What we do not yet know: how many people have been removed without final orders since January 2025, whether the pattern concentrates in specific detention circuits, and whether habeas remedies are functioning at scale or only for the rare cases that reach federal court.

Credit where due: the Deportation Data Project, led by David Hausman and collaborators, is doing some of the most important independent data work on removals. Their FOIA spreadsheets are the reason these cases are visible at all.

NY1 sent the data to EOIR before publishing. A spokesperson declined to comment on third-party analysis of EOIR data. DOJ did not respond to questions about the Salvadoran man's case. Outside reporting and FOIA work is effectively the only audit available right now.

The deportations are happening faster than the legal architecture was built to process. ICE's stated removal target is 3,000 per day. Roughly 60,000 people are currently detained. The administrative mechanisms designed to secure due process are being bypassed or outrun.

Sheila McNulty served 16 years at DOJ and was Chief Immigration Judge when she was dismissed on the first day of Trump's second term. She told NY1 she does not know the legal basis for deporting people without final orders: "I'm not sure where the authority is."

One case: a Salvadoran man with Special Immigrant Juvenile Status and a pending green card was arrested in New York, flown to Texas, and deported to El Salvador with no final removal order on record. His attorney, Ed Cuccia, described the removal as unlawful.

Noncitizens are being deported without final removal orders, which immigration attorneys say is flatly illegal. Lawyers in New York, Louisiana, Texas, and Illinois have reported such cases to NY1. At least two of the documented deportations occurred in New York City.

The full breakdown of the Tobay Robles case, the history of habeas corpus, and what a de facto suspension of due process looks like in practice is here: austinkocher.substack.com/p/the-soft-s...
What the data doesn't yet tell us: how often courts are actually enforcing these orders versus issuing them and moving on. Contempt threats are meaningful but only if they're followed through.

I saw a similar spike in habeas cases at the start of COVID-19, when ICE detention centers became dangerous infection sites. The mechanism is the same: a surge in enforcement without legal safeguards forces people into court. This spike is larger.

In the Minnesota case, Judge Patrick Schiltz took the U.S. Attorney to task for what he described as an embarrassing response to court concerns. When judges appointed by Republican presidents threaten contempt, that tells you something.

Habeas corpus is the legal mechanism that lets people challenge whether their detention is lawful. It's in Article 1 of the Constitution. The administration has openly discussed suspending it and may not need to if agencies can simply ignore court orders.
A federal judge in Minnesota threatened criminal contempt against the U.S. Attorney's office for ignoring a habeas corpus order in an ICE detention case.

I spoke with Zain Lakhani of the Women's Refugee Commission about all of this. It's one of the most important conversations I've had this year. Full transcript and audio here: austinkocher.substack.com/p/ice-is-vio...

We don't yet know the full scale of postpartum and lactating women being detained in violation of ICE's own policies. WRC has built a pregnancy detention tracker with RelevantResearch and this data is still being collected.

There is no legal right to family reunification under U.S. law and no DHS procedure for facilitating it. More than 400 parents sought reunification through Honduran government channels. The report calls for building that system from scratch.

One case from the report: a woman experienced a miscarriage in detention, received no medical oversight for ten days, was deported in an acute medical crisis, and was only saved because reception workers in Honduras rushed her to an emergency room.

ICE's own Detained Parents Directive requires agents to ask every arrestee if they're a parent, to ensure children are safe, and to give parents a choice about whether children accompany them. The report documents routine violations of all three requirements.
Under Biden, 264 mothers were detained and 30% were deported. Under Trump, that's jumped to 800 mothers detained and 60% deported.
